title: Can you solve these 13 case interview maths questions in your head?
description: Practice sums for case interviews: margins, percentages, growth and big numbers, with worked answers hidden until you are ready.
hook: The best way to get comfortable with case maths is to do lots of small sums. Here is a set of practice questions to try in your head, with the answers hidden until you are ready.
body:
1. A product costs $40 and sells for $50. What's the margin? The markup?

Show the answer

Margin = 10/50 = 20%. Markup = 10/40 = 25%.

2. Fixed costs $3M, price $25, variable cost $10. Breakeven units?

Show the answer

3M ÷ 15 = 200,000 units.

3. Revenue grows from $50M to $80M in 5 years. CAGR roughly?

Show the answer

1.6^(1/5) ≈ 9.9% → ~10%.

4. A machine costs $1.2M and saves $300k a year. Payback?

Show the answer

4 years.

5. Perpetuity: $5M a year, discount rate 8%. Value?

Show the answer

5 ÷ 0.08 = $62.5M.

6. Price up 10%, volume down 5%. Revenue change?

Show the answer

1.10 × 0.95 = 1.045 → +4.5%.

7. Monthly churn 2%. Average customer lifetime?

Show the answer

1 ÷ 0.02 = 50 months.

8. 50% chance of $10M, 30% of $2M, 20% of −$5M. Expected value?

Show the answer

5 + 0.6 − 1 = $4.6M.

9. What is 17% of 340?

Show the answer

34 + 23.8 = 57.8 (10% + 7%).

10. $4.5B ÷ 1.5M customers?

Show the answer

$3,000 per customer.

11. What is 15% of 480?

Show the answer

72. 10% = 48, 5% = 24, total 72.

12. Fixed costs $3M, price $25, variable cost $10. Breakeven volume?

Show the answer

200,000. Contribution = $15. $3M ÷ $15 = 200,000 units.

13. Cost $80, price $100. Which is true?

Show the answer

Margin 20%, markup 25%. Margin is on price (20/100); markup is on cost (20/80).

A tougher two-step drill

A subscription business has 80,000 paying customers at £15 per month. It adds 5,000 new customers in the month but loses 4% of opening customers. How many customers are left, and what would monthly recurring revenue be at the same price?

<details><summary>Show the solution</summary><p>Churned customers = 80,000 × 4% = 3,200. Closing customers = 80,000 + 5,000 − 3,200 = <b>81,800</b>. Closing monthly recurring revenue = 81,800 × £15 = <b>£1,227,000</b>. This uses the ending customer count as a snapshot, not actual recognised revenue across the month.</p></details>

The trap is calculating 4% churn on the ending base or calling the ending monthly run-rate "revenue earned this month". In a case, state whether a number is a period flow or a point-in-time stock.
outro: For timed practice, try the free case maths drill. Next in this topic: How do you do case interview maths out loud without panicking?
